newsitem.title: ZAIRE: New Zaire PM offers rebels six cabinet posts.
newsitem.headline: New Zaire PM offers rebels six cabinet posts.

text.p: Zaire's new Prime Minister Etienne Tshisekedi unveiled a cabinet on Thursday with no associates of President Mobutu Sese Seko and six ministries reserved for rebels controlling a quarter of the country.
But a rebel official said the rebels would not join Tshisekedi's government.

Asked by reporters as he boarded a plane in the Zairean city of Goma for talks in South Africa whether the rebel alliance would accept the posts reserved for the rebels, Raphael Nghenda, rebel information commissioner, said without elaborating: "No".
In what local analysts described as a new front against the ailing and embattled Mobutu, opposition leader Tshisekedi also dissolved parliament which is dominated by Mobutu's supporters.
Its legislative role would revert to the sovereign national conference that launched Zaire's democratic transition seven years ago and, in theory, stripped Mobutu of most powers.
"Tshisekedi has opened a second front against Mobutu," said a local commentator, referring to advances by Laurent Kabila's rebels who have put Mobutu's army on the run in eastern Zaire.
"I don't think Mobutu will accept this and Zaire could be headed for a probably worse political crisis in Kinshasa," said the analyst who asked not to be identified.
"He has no power to dissolve parliament. It is madness," said Banza Mukalayi, vice-president of Mobutu's Popular Revolutionary Movement (MPR) ruling party.
Banza told Reuters the Mobutu camp would react strongly.

Tshisekedi, who announced details of the 26-member government at a news conference, said the portfolios of foreign affairs, defence, budget, planning, foreign trade and agriculture were reserved for the rebel alliance.
He showered praise on Kabila, whose rebels have seized a quarter of Zaire and are targeting mainstay mining centres after launching a rebellion from the Rwandan border in October.

"Kabila has contributed to the return of legality. He merits the acclaim of our people," Tshisekedi said, adding that the rebel leader took up arms because of Mobutu's "violation of the decisions of the national conference".
But he said the civil war now had to stop.
"I don't see the war continuing. Too much Zairean blood has been shed. I will see my brother Kabila and discuss," he said.
Tshisekedi has never accepted his 1993 sacking from the post by Mobutu after his appointment as prime minister by the national conference in 1991.
The national conference dissolved itself in December 1992 to make way for a High Council of the Republic, which in turn evolved into the transitional parliament in 1994.
The transitional parliament nominated Tshisekedi on Tuesday after Kengo wa Dondo, who was appointed in 1994 and had strongly backed the military option in the war, resigned.
Mobutu ratified the appointment of Tshisekedi, a veteran opponent who has called for talks with the rebels from early in the conflict, on Wednesday.
France expressed hope on Thursday that the appointment of Tshisekedi would lead to fruitful negotiations with the rebels.
"We have noted the appointment of Etienne Tshisekedi as the new head of the Zairean government," the French Foreign Ministry said in a statement on Thursday.
"This should create a propitious climate for intra-Zairean negotiations which are to begin at the end of the week in South Africa," the statement said.
Meanwhile, Rwandan Hutu refugees left eastern Zaire by truck for Rwanda as aid agencies struggled to reach 80,000 more scattered deeper in the Zairean interior.
Filippo Grandi, east Zaire representative of the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), said 4,800 refugees were repatriated by trucks from Karuba west of Goma on Tuesday and Wednesday.

Mobutu, who has cancer, has seen his grip on the sprawling Central African nation weakened by rebel advances. The rebels took up arms in October in a dispute over Zairean nationality for ethnic Tutsis. They say Mobutu must stand down.
